 Greater Boston Food Bank expects to distribute a record amount of food for the holidays
 Amanda Beland 
 Tiziana Dearing 
 November 18, 2026 Share Greater Boston Food Bank warehouse. (Courtesy/Greater Boston Food Bank) The Greater Boston Food Bank is planning to distribute a record amount of food this holiday season due to federal policy changes and a rising cost of living.
 “The Greater Boston Food Bank has been providing food to hungry families for over 45 years,” said Kathryn Alexander, the food bank’s vice president of external affairs. “Our work has only grown … we have only fed more and more people.”
 This year, the food bank expects to distribute over 54,000 turkeys — the most in its history and 4,000 more than last year. Charlie Bumpus runs GBFB’s warehouse operations. He said the holiday season is tough because they aren’t just delivering turkeys.
 “It's all of the other components that go with a holiday meal,” Bumpus said. “They increase as well, and we're still serving all the same food that we normally would serve. We don't cut back just 'cause it's a holiday.”
 Bumpus said demand for all food is up and that means his team of 25 is working hard to get food sorted and out of the warehouse. The GBFB delivered about 4 million more meals in its last fiscal year (which ended in September) than in the previous one, according to the organization. Only in 2021 — the first year after the pandemic — did the bank distribute more food than they are right now.
 The higher demand for food is largely due to changes to the Supplemental Nutrition and Assistance Program (SNAP), formerly called food stamps. Last summer, Congress approved changes to who qualifies for assistance and shifted more responsibility onto states for funding the program. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates over 180,000 people have lost SNAP benefits since last fall.
 Alexander said this impact is about more than just food — it can disrupt all areas of somebody’s life.
 “When they get SNAP, they have more money to put to a medical bill,” she said. “They have more money to pay for rent or put toward their mortgage. When that money's gone, [they] then have less to spend at the grocery store.”
 At the same time, more people are saying they don’t have regular access to healthy food. Bumpus said higher demand means the GBFB has had to adapt. One way they’ve done that is by expanding their cooler space, so they can hold and then distribute more dairy, eggs, and fresh produce. The change allowed them to distribute over 35 million pounds of produce last fiscal year, the most they’ve ever delivered.
 “The team here is just amazing,” he said. “We just do our work, and at the end of the day when these guys are hurting at the end of the week, especially after lifting so much, they're always happy.”
 Alexander said the bank is worried that upcoming changes to Medicaid could drive up even more need in the coming months. She said the GBFB is hopeful that when a new Congress takes over next year that they will reverse the changes to SNAP that have left many people without enough food to eat.
 “At the end of the day, SNAP is our greatest defense against hunger,” she said. “It is a proven tool to enable people to feed themselves and to care for themselves. It is a bridge out of poverty.”
 This segment aired on November 18, 2026. Audio will be available soon.
